images.caption: Building detail of Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan
images.desc: Stand in Registan Square and it's easy to see why it is considered the architectural heart of Samarkand—one of Central Asia's oldest cities. This plaza in Uzbekistan is framed by three magnificent madrasas—Islamic centres of learning—whose soaring portals draw the eye upwards. Yet some of the square's greatest treasures reveal themselves only when you look closer.

images.title: The fish that outgrew its name
images.caption: International Whale Shark Day
images.desc: Today, International Whale Shark Day makes room for the world's largest fish. Despite their name, whale sharks are not whales but fish, reaching lengths of up to 18 metres and weighing around 18 tonnes. Found in warm tropical seas, they glide through the water with their mouths open, filtering plankton, fish eggs and other tiny prey. This species' distinctive white-spot patterns are unique to each individual, much like human fingerprints.

images.title: Where tides shape a legend
images.caption: Mont-Saint‑Michel during high tide, Normandy, France
images.desc: At sunset, Mont-Saint‑Michel rises from the waters of Normandy, France, like a fortress shaped by the sea. Perched on a rocky tidal island, the abbey and village stand at the centre of one of Europe's most dramatic coastal settings. Twice a day, the sea retreats to reveal vast stretches of sand before surging back to reclaim the landscape. At high tide, the mount becomes an island once again. For centuries, travellers timed their journeys to this rhythm, crossing the flats when conditions allowed and watching the sea return hours later.

images.title: Water, wildlife and wonder
images.caption: World Lake Day
images.desc: Imagine a world without the natural wonders that hold about 90% of Earth's surface freshwater. Lakes are among our planet's most valuable resources, providing clean water, supporting wildlife, regulating climate and sustaining communities worldwide. Recognising their importance, the United Nations designated 27 August as World Lake Day, first observed in 2025. Earth is home to more than 117 million lakes covering nearly 4% of its land surface. Together, they sustain countless ecosystems, while Lake Baikal in Russia alone holds about one-fifth of the world's surface liquid freshwater. Yet many lakes face growing pressure from pollution, overuse and climate change.

images.title: A sky alive with colour
images.caption: Auroras over Kirkjufell, Iceland
images.desc: As darker nights return to Iceland, visitors will soon look to the skies for a chance to see the aurora borealis. Better known as the northern lights, this luminous phenomenon occurs when charged particles from the sun collide with oxygen and nitrogen high in Earth's atmosphere, creating shimmering ribbons of green, pink, purple and sometimes red light. From September to April, Iceland's northern location and long winter nights make it one of the world's finest places to witness the display.

images.title: Crossing into history
images.caption: Brooklyn Bridge, New York City, United States
images.desc: The Brooklyn Bridge doesn't just connect Manhattan and Brooklyn in the United States—it bridges history, engineering and a few surprising stories too. Opened in 1883 after 14 years of construction, it became the world's first steel-wire suspension bridge, forever changing the way New Yorkers crossed the East River.
